tiles.title: Filtering Rows with WHERE and Logical Operators
tiles.summary: Learn to filter query results with WHERE, combine conditions using AND, OR, and NOT, control evaluation order with parentheses, and test for missing values with IS NULL.

steps.title: Filtering rows with WHERE
steps.lede: Ask a question of your data by keeping only the rows where a condition is true.

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM orders returns every order in the QuickCart database. To answer a real question — which orders took longer than 40 minutes to deliver? — you need to narrow the result to just the matching rows. WHERE takes a search condition and evaluates it for every row. A row is kept only if the condition is true; rows where it is false are discarded.

The comparison operators <, >, <=, >=, =, and <> compare two values of the same or a compatible type and produce a boolean result. = tests for equal; <> tests for not equal (!= is an alias for <>). WHERE customer_id = 2 keeps only orders from customer 2; WHERE delivery_time_minutes <> 20 keeps orders whose delivery time is not 20 minutes.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40

after.caption: After WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40 — only rows where the condition is true

blocks.change_summary: WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40 keeps only the five orders whose delivery time exceeds 40 minutes; the other rows are discarded.

steps.title: Combining conditions with AND, OR, and NOT
steps.lede: Join multiple filter conditions to express precise requirements.

blocks.text: A WHERE clause often needs more than one condition at once — for example, orders from customer 1 that also took longer than 30 minutes. AND, OR, and NOT let you combine boolean conditions. AND is true only when both sides are true; OR is true when at least one side is true; NOT reverses a true or false value.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2

left.caption: Without parentheses: AND binds first, then OR

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 AND (delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2)

right.caption: With parentheses: OR is evaluated first inside the group

blocks.takeaway: The same three conditions produce different result sets depending on where the parentheses go — AND always binds before OR unless you override it.

steps.title: Evaluation order and parentheses
steps.lede: NOT binds tightest, then AND, then OR — use parentheses to override.

blocks.text: Without parentheses, NOT is evaluated before AND, and AND before OR. WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2 is read as (customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30) OR customer_id = 2, keeping any order from customer 2 regardless of delivery time.

Parentheses force a different evaluation order. WHERE customer_id = 1 AND (delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2) evaluates the OR first; because customer_id = 1 already rules out customer_id = 2, this version keeps only customer 1 orders that took longer than 30 minutes. NOT reverses a condition: WHERE NOT (customer_id = 1) keeps every order not from customer 1.

steps.lede: Trace the default evaluation order to predict which rows a query returns.

steps.title: Testing for missing values with IS NULL
steps.lede: Missing values are unknown — use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL, never = NULL.

blocks.text: Some orders in the QuickCart database have no recorded delivery time — the value is missing, not zero. SQL represents a missing value with NULL. NULL means unknown: it is not known whether two unknown values are equal, so testing for NULL with an ordinary comparison operator does not work.

To test whether a value is or is not null, use the predicates IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL finds the orders with a missing delivery time; WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NOT NULL finds the rest.

Writing WHERE delivery_time_minutes = NULL does not test for null. NULL is not considered 'equal to' NULL, so that comparison never evaluates to true, and the query silently returns zero rows instead of the missing-time orders you meant to find.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes = NULL

before.caption: WHERE delivery_time_minutes = NULL — returns no rows (= NULL never evaluates to true)

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL

after.caption: WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL — returns the two orders with a missing delivery time

blocks.change_summary: Replacing = NULL with IS NULL returns the rows with a missing delivery time; = NULL silently returns nothing because NULL is not considered equal to NULL.

steps.title: Recap: Filtering Rows
steps.lede: Three tools for precise row selection: WHERE, logical operators, and IS NULL.

blocks.text: WHERE evaluates a condition for every row and keeps only those where it is true. Comparison operators (<, >, <=, >=, =, <>) produce the boolean result. AND, OR, and NOT combine conditions; AND binds before OR unless you add parentheses. NULL means unknown — use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test for missing values; = NULL never matches.

blocks.title: Next: Sorting Results with ORDER BY
blocks.text: WHERE decides which rows come back, but not what order they appear in. Next you will use ORDER BY to sort results from slowest to fastest delivery — or any other direction you need.

remediation_steps.title: Comparison operators: which one to use
remediation_steps.lede: Each comparison operator tests a different relationship between two values.

blocks.text: The six comparison operators are <, >, <=, >=, =, and <>. = tests whether two values are equal; <> (or !=) tests whether they are not equal. < and > test strict less-than and greater-than; <= and >= include the boundary value. WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40 keeps rows where the time is strictly above 40; WHERE delivery_time_minutes >= 40 would also keep a row with exactly 40 minutes.

remediation_steps.title: How WHERE evaluates each row
remediation_steps.lede: WHERE tests the condition against every row and keeps only those where it is true.

blocks.text: WHERE takes a search condition and evaluates it for each row in the table. A row is kept only if the condition evaluates to true; rows where it is false are discarded. SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 2 keeps only the rows where customer_id equals 2 and discards every other row.

remediation_steps.title: Which rows does WHERE keep?
remediation_steps.lede: WHERE keeps a row only when the condition is true for that row.

blocks.text: Think of WHERE as a row-by-row question: for each row, is this condition true? If yes, the row appears in the result. If no, it is discarded. WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40 asks that question for every order in the QuickCart table and returns only the orders where the delivery time is above 40 minutes.

remediation_steps.title: Default evaluation order: NOT, then AND, then OR
remediation_steps.lede: Without parentheses, AND always binds before OR — which can change the rows you get.

blocks.text: When you write multiple conditions without parentheses, SQL evaluates NOT first, then AND, then OR. WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2 is treated as (customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30) OR customer_id = 2. That keeps every order from customer 2, regardless of delivery time — which may not be what you intended.

remediation_steps.title: Using parentheses to control AND/OR grouping
remediation_steps.lede: Parentheses override the default precedence so the OR is evaluated where you need it.

blocks.text: AND, OR, and NOT combine boolean conditions. AND is true only when both sides are true; OR is true when at least one side is true. By default AND binds before OR. Adding parentheses forces the OR to be evaluated first: WHERE customer_id = 1 AND (delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2) evaluates the OR group first, then applies the AND — giving a different result set.

remediation_steps.title: AND, OR, and NOT: combining conditions
remediation_steps.lede: Use AND to require both conditions, OR to accept either, and NOT to exclude.

blocks.text: AND requires both conditions to be true: WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 keeps only customer 1's slow orders. OR accepts either: WHERE customer_id = 1 OR customer_id = 2 keeps orders from either customer. NOT reverses a condition: WHERE NOT (customer_id = 1) keeps every order that is not from customer 1.

remediation_steps.title: Why = NULL never matches
remediation_steps.lede: NULL means unknown — and an unknown value is not considered equal to anything, including another unknown.

blocks.text: NULL represents an unknown value. It is not known whether two unknown values are equal, so the comparison delivery_time_minutes = NULL never evaluates to true — not even when the value is actually missing. The query runs without error but silently returns zero rows, which is not what you want when looking for missing delivery times.

remediation_steps.title: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL: the right predicates
remediation_steps.lede: Use IS NULL to find missing values and IS NOT NULL to find present ones.

blocks.text: To test whether a value is missing, use IS NULL. To test whether a value is present, use IS NOT NULL. WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL returns the orders with no recorded delivery time; WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NOT NULL returns the orders that do have one. Together these two predicates cover the whole table.

steps.title: Controlling the order of your results with ORDER BY
steps.lede: A WHERE clause decides which orders come back, but not what order they appear in. ORDER BY gives you that control.

blocks.text: ORDER BY sorts result rows by the expression you name. If you don't specify a direction, ascending (ASC) order is assumed by default — so `ORDER BY delivery_time_minutes` lists the fastest QuickCart deliveries first. Add DESC to reverse it: `ORDER BY delivery_time_minutes DESC` puts the slowest deliveries at the top.

When two rows tie on the first sort expression, SQL compares them on the next one. `ORDER BY customer_id, delivery_time_minutes DESC` groups each customer's orders together (ascending by customer_id) and within each customer shows the slowest delivery first. You can chain as many tiebreaker columns as you need.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id ASC, delivery_time_minutes DESC

after.caption: After ORDER BY customer_id ASC, delivery_time_minutes DESC

blocks.change_summary: Adding ORDER BY customer_id ASC, delivery_time_minutes DESC groups rows by customer and within each customer shows the slowest delivery first.

steps.title: Returning a slice of rows with LIMIT and OFFSET
steps.lede: Once results are sorted, LIMIT and OFFSET let you take just the rows you need — the top five, or the next page.

blocks.text: LIMIT restricts the maximum number of rows a query returns. OFFSET specifies how many rows to skip before returning rows. `SELECT order_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders ORDER BY delivery_time_minutes DESC LIMIT 3` returns the three slowest deliveries in the QuickCart dataset.

When both are specified, OFFSET rows are skipped first, then up to LIMIT rows of what remains are returned. Adding `OFFSET 3` to that same query skips the three slowest and returns the next three — a second page of results.
Without ORDER BY, LIMIT and OFFSET return an unpredictable subset. SQL promises no particular sequence unless ORDER BY is present.

blocks.alt_text: A sorted list passes through an OFFSET step that discards the first rows, then a LIMIT step that keeps the next rows, producing the final output.

steps.title: Sorting and limiting results
steps.lede: Two clauses that shape what comes back and in what order.

blocks.text: ORDER BY sorts result rows by one or more expressions. Omitting a direction defaults to ASC; add DESC to reverse. A second column in ORDER BY breaks ties on the first.
LIMIT caps the number of rows returned; OFFSET skips rows before the limit is applied. Always pair them with ORDER BY — without it the subset returned is unpredictable.

blocks.title: Up next: Aggregating Data with GROUP BY
blocks.text: Next you'll collapse many rows into summary numbers using COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX — and group those summaries by category with GROUP BY.

remediation_steps.title: How ORDER BY handles tied values
remediation_steps.lede: When two rows are equal on the first sort column, SQL moves to the next one.

blocks.text: If two rows are equal according to the leftmost ORDER BY expression, SQL compares them on the next expression. `ORDER BY customer_id ASC, delivery_time_minutes DESC` first groups rows by customer_id; within each customer group, the row with the longest delivery time appears first. Without a second column, tied rows appear in an unspecified order.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (1,2) ORDER BY customer_id ASC, delivery_time_minutes DESC

blocks.caption: Customers 1 and 2 sorted by customer_id ASC, delivery_time_minutes DESC — ties on customer_id broken by delivery time

remediation_steps.title: OFFSET skips first, then LIMIT keeps
remediation_steps.lede: The two clauses work in sequence: skip, then keep.

blocks.text: When both OFFSET and LIMIT are present, OFFSET rows are skipped first, and then up to LIMIT rows of what remains are returned. On a 13-row orders table sorted by amount DESC: `LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3` skips the three highest-amount orders and returns the next three.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3

blocks.caption: LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3 on orders sorted by amount DESC — rows 4–6 of the sorted list

steps.title: Collapsing many rows into one number with aggregate functions
steps.lede: So far your queries returned one row per record. Aggregate functions let you compute a single summary across all of them.

blocks.text: Aggregate functions compute a single result from a set of input values — many rows in, one value out. `COUNT(*)` counts every input row; `COUNT(delivery_time_minutes)` counts only the rows where that column is not null, so it skips the two undelivered QuickCart orders.

The other four functions all ignore nulls. `SUM(delivery_time_minutes)` totals the non-null delivery times; `AVG` computes their arithmetic mean; `MIN` finds the shortest delivery; `MAX` finds the longest. One SELECT can compute all five at once, returning a single row of summary numbers.

before.caption: orders — one row per order, delivery_time_minutes shown (two NULLs)

result_of.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_orders, COUNT(delivery_time_minutes) AS delivered_orders, SUM(delivery_time_minutes) AS total_minutes, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_minutes, MIN(delivery_time_minutes) AS min_minutes, MAX(delivery_time_minutes) AS max_minutes FROM orders

after.caption: After COUNT(*), COUNT(col), SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX — one summary row, NULLs skipped by all except COUNT(*)

blocks.change_summary: Aggregate functions collapse all rows into a single summary row. COUNT(*) includes NULLs in the row count; the others skip them.

steps.title: Splitting rows into groups with GROUP BY
steps.lede: A single AVG gives one number for all orders combined. GROUP BY lets you compute that average separately for each customer or region.

blocks.text: GROUP BY groups together rows that share the same values in the listed columns, combining each group into one output row. Any aggregate function in the SELECT list is then computed separately within each group. `SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id` returns one row per customer_id, each showing that customer's own average delivery time.

When a table is grouped, any column not listed in GROUP BY cannot appear in the SELECT list except inside an aggregate function. `SELECT customer_id, order_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id` would fail because order_id is neither grouped nor aggregated — each customer group contains several different order_ids, so SQL cannot pick one.

blocks.title: GROUP BY customer_id: rows split into per-customer buckets
blocks.alt_text: All orders rows are split into three buckets by customer_id. Each bucket collapses into one output row showing that customer's average delivery time.

steps.title: Filtering aggregated groups with HAVING
steps.lede: WHERE filters raw rows before grouping. To filter on an aggregate result — keeping only customers whose average delivery time is high — you need HAVING.

blocks.text: HAVING filters out groups after GROUP BY has combined rows and computed aggregates. It acts on groups rather than raw rows, much like WHERE acts on rows. `SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING AVG(delivery_time_minutes) > 30` keeps only the customer groups whose average delivery time exceeds 30 minutes.

Expressions in HAVING can refer to grouped columns and to aggregate expressions computed over the group. You can use both in the same clause: `HAVING customer_id > 1 AND AVG(delivery_time_minutes) > 30` mixes a grouped column and an aggregate. WHERE and HAVING can also appear in the same query — WHERE removes raw rows before grouping, HAVING then filters the grouped result.

blocks.title: WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING: the filtering pipeline
blocks.alt_text: A pipeline: raw rows pass through WHERE (removes rows), then GROUP BY (forms groups), then HAVING (removes groups), producing the final result.

steps.title: Aggregating data with GROUP BY
steps.lede: Three tools that turn rows into summaries.

blocks.text: Aggregate functions — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX — compute one value from many rows. The shape is always the same: many row values in, one summary value out.
GROUP BY answers 'per X' questions: list the grouping column, and each aggregate is computed once per bucket instead of once overall.
HAVING filters groups after aggregation, just as WHERE filters rows before grouping. Use WHERE to narrow raw rows, HAVING to narrow the grouped result.

blocks.title: Up next: CASE Expressions
blocks.text: Next you'll add conditional logic inside a query — labelling each order as 'fast', 'normal' or 'slow' based on its delivery time using CASE WHEN … THEN … ELSE … END.

remediation_steps.title: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) skips NULLs
remediation_steps.lede: The two forms of COUNT give different answers when a column has missing values.

blocks.text: COUNT(*) counts every input row regardless of nulls. COUNT(expression) counts only the rows where that expression is not null. The orders table has 13 rows but two have a NULL delivery_time_minutes — so COUNT(*) returns 13 while COUNT(delivery_time_minutes) returns 11.

result_of.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(delivery_time_minutes) AS delivered FROM orders

blocks.caption: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(delivery_time_minutes) — the difference equals the number of NULL delivery times

remediation_steps.title: SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX — which question each answers
remediation_steps.lede: Each function answers a different kind of question about a set of values.

blocks.text: SUM totals the non-null values — use it for 'what is the combined amount'. AVG computes the arithmetic mean — use it for 'what is the typical value'. MIN finds the smallest non-null value — use it for 'what is the fastest delivery'. MAX finds the largest — use it for 'what is the slowest delivery'. All four skip NULLs.

remediation_steps.title: Every SELECT column must be grouped or aggregated
remediation_steps.lede: When GROUP BY is present, SQL enforces a strict rule about which columns can appear in SELECT.

blocks.text: When a table is grouped, a column not listed in GROUP BY cannot appear in the SELECT list except inside an aggregate function. Each customer group contains several order_ids, so SQL cannot pick one to show — the query `SELECT customer_id, order_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id` fails. Fix it by removing order_id or wrapping it in an aggregate such as COUNT(order_id).

remediation_steps.title: HAVING expressions can reference grouped columns and aggregates
remediation_steps.lede: HAVING is more flexible than WHERE — it can test both the grouping column and any aggregate.

blocks.text: Expressions in HAVING can refer to grouped columns and to aggregate expressions computed over the group. For example, `HAVING customer_id > 1 AND AVG(delivery_time_minutes) > 30` tests a grouped column (customer_id) and an aggregate (AVG) in the same clause. WHERE cannot reference aggregates at all — that is why HAVING exists.

steps.title: Labelling rows with CASE WHEN … THEN … END
steps.lede: Sometimes a query needs a label computed per row — calling each order 'fast', 'normal' or 'slow' based on its delivery time.

blocks.text: A CASE WHEN condition THEN result … END expression evaluates its WHEN conditions in order and returns the result of the first one that is true. The conditions are tested top to bottom; once one matches, the rest are skipped.

blocks.code:
SELECT
  order_id,
  delivery_time_minutes,
  CASE
    WHEN delivery_time_minutes < 20 THEN 'fast'    -- branch 1
    WHEN delivery_time_minutes < 40 THEN 'normal'  -- branch 2
    ELSE 'slow'                                     -- fallback
  END AS speed
FROM orders

annotations.text: CASE starts the expression; conditions are tested in the order they appear.
Branch 1: if delivery_time_minutes < 20, return 'fast' and stop.
Branch 2: only reached if branch 1 was false. Returns 'normal' for times 20–39.
ELSE is the fallback for any row that matched no WHEN condition.
END closes the CASE expression; AS speed names the output column.

steps.title: What happens when no WHEN matches — and the simple CASE form
steps.lede: If no condition is true, CASE returns the ELSE value. Omit ELSE and it returns NULL. There is also a shorter form for equality checks.

blocks.text: If no WHEN condition is true, CASE returns the ELSE result if given, or NULL if ELSE is omitted. A row with a NULL delivery_time_minutes also falls through to ELSE, since no WHEN condition is true for a null. Omitting ELSE can silently produce NULLs.

CASE also has a simpler form for equality comparisons: `CASE expression WHEN value THEN result … END` compares one expression against each listed value directly. `CASE city WHEN 'Lagos' THEN 'south' WHEN 'Kano' THEN 'north' ELSE 'other' END` compares city to each city value instead of writing a full condition each time. Use this form when all branches test the same expression for equality.

steps.lede: Confirm you understand that WHEN conditions are tested in order and the first match wins.

steps.title: Conditional logic with CASE expressions
steps.lede: CASE lets you compute a per-row label or value based on conditions.

blocks.text: CASE WHEN condition THEN result … END evaluates conditions in order and returns the first match. If no condition matches, ELSE provides a fallback; without ELSE the result is NULL. A NULL input value falls through to ELSE because no WHEN condition is true for it.
The simple form — CASE expression WHEN value THEN result … END — is a shorthand for equality checks against one expression. Use it when all branches compare the same column to different values.

blocks.title: Up next: SQL Style Conventions
blocks.text: Next you'll learn formatting and naming conventions that make SQL queries easier to read and maintain — keyword casing, indentation and alias style.

remediation_steps.title: WHEN conditions are tested in order — first match wins
remediation_steps.lede: The order of WHEN branches matters: SQL stops at the first true condition.

blocks.text: A CASE expression evaluates its WHEN conditions from top to bottom and returns the result of the first one that is true. Once a branch matches, the remaining branches are not tested. In `CASE WHEN delivery_time_minutes < 20 THEN 'fast' WHEN delivery_time_minutes < 40 THEN 'normal' ELSE 'slow' END`, an order with delivery_time_minutes = 15 matches the first branch and is labelled 'fast' — the second branch is never evaluated for that row.

remediation_steps.title: No WHEN match → ELSE result, or NULL if ELSE is absent
remediation_steps.lede: What CASE returns when none of its conditions are true depends on whether ELSE is present.

blocks.text: If no WHEN condition is true, CASE returns the ELSE result if one is given, or NULL if ELSE is omitted. A row with a NULL delivery_time_minutes also falls through to ELSE, because `NULL < 20` and `NULL < 40` are both not true. Omitting ELSE is valid but can silently produce NULLs in the output column.

tiles.title: SQL Style Conventions
tiles.summary: Format SQL queries consistently: uppercase keywords, lowercase columns, meaningful aliases with AS, right-aligned keyword 'river', and one clause per line.

steps.title: SQL style conventions
steps.lede: Consistent formatting makes queries easier to read, review, and debug.

blocks.text: Reserved keywords — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, AND, OR — should always be written in uppercase. Column names should always be written in lowercase, except where it makes sense not to, such as proper nouns. So SELECT customer_id, city FROM customers WHERE city = 'Lagos' follows the convention; a mix like select Customer_ID from Customers where City = 'Lagos' does not.

An alias name should relate to the object it aliases — as a rule of thumb, the first letter of each word in the object's name — and the AS keyword should always be included: FROM orders AS o, not FROM orders o or FROM orders AS x. Each root keyword starts a new line and is right-aligned so all keywords end on the same character boundary (a 'river'). Values sit left-aligned after them; spaces go around '=' and after commas; a newline comes before AND or OR so each condition starts its own line.

before.code: select customer_id,city from customers where city='Lagos' and customer_id>1

annotations.text: Keywords lowercase, column names lowercase, no line breaks, no spaces around operators

after.code:
SELECT customer_id, city
    FROM customers
   WHERE city = 'Lagos'
     AND customer_id > 1

annotations.text: Keywords uppercase; column names lowercase
FROM starts a new line, right-aligned to the 'river'
WHERE starts a new line; spaces around '='
AND on its own line, right-aligned

steps.lede: Five rules that keep every query readable at a glance.

blocks.text: Write reserved keywords in uppercase and column names in lowercase. Alias with AS and choose a name derived from the object — FROM orders AS o. Right-align root keywords to form a 'river', put each clause on its own line, and place a newline before AND or OR so every condition is easy to scan.

blocks.title: Next: Text and Date Functions
blocks.text: Now that your queries are consistently formatted, you will learn to transform the values inside them — cleaning city names with LOWER and TRIM, building labels with CONCAT, and pulling date parts with EXTRACT.

remediation_steps.title: The keyword 'river' and line-break rules
remediation_steps.lede: Right-align keywords to form a 'river'; put each clause and each AND/OR condition on its own line.

blocks.text: Each root keyword — SELECT, FROM, WHERE — starts its own line and is right-aligned so all keywords end on the same character boundary, forming a vertical 'river'. Values sit left-aligned after them on the same line. Spaces go before and after '=' and after every comma. A newline always comes before AND or OR so each condition starts its own line: WHERE city = 'Lagos' / AND customer_id > 1, not WHERE city = 'Lagos' AND customer_id > 1 on one line.

remediation_steps.title: Keyword and column casing
remediation_steps.lede: Keywords uppercase, column names lowercase — every time.

blocks.text: Reserved keywords — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, AND, OR, AS, GROUP BY, ORDER BY — should always be uppercase. Column names should always be lowercase, except proper nouns. SELECT customer_id, city FROM customers WHERE city = 'Lagos' is correct; select Customer_ID from Customers where City = 'Lagos' breaks both rules.

remediation_steps.title: Writing a conventional alias
remediation_steps.lede: Use AS and choose an alias name derived from the object's name.

blocks.text: An alias name should relate to the object it aliases. As a rule of thumb, use the first letter of each word in the object's name: orders → o, order_items → oi, customers → c. Always include the AS keyword to make the alias explicit: FROM orders AS o, not FROM orders o or FROM orders AS x.

tiles.title: Text and Date Functions
tiles.summary: Clean and transform text with LOWER, UPPER, TRIM, CONCAT, and LENGTH; extract date parts with EXTRACT and compute elapsed days; convert types with CAST and :: syntax.

steps.title: Cleaning text with LOWER, UPPER, TRIM, CONCAT, and LENGTH
steps.lede: Four functions that clean, combine, and measure text values in a query.

blocks.text: LOWER(text) converts a string to all lower case; UPPER(text) converts it to all upper case. LOWER(city) turns 'LAGOS' or 'Lagos' into 'lagos', which is useful for comparing city names that were entered inconsistently.

TRIM removes leading or trailing spaces (by default) from a string — TRIM(city) strips accidental spaces from a city value. CONCAT joins its arguments into one string and ignores any NULL arguments: CONCAT(name, ' (', city, ')') builds a single label. LENGTH(text) returns the number of characters: LENGTH(name) gives the character count of a customer's name.

result_of.sql: SELECT customer_id, name, LOWER(TRIM(city)) AS city FROM customers

after.caption: After LOWER(TRIM(city)) — consistent lowercase, casing standardised

blocks.change_summary: LOWER(TRIM(city)) standardises city values to consistent lowercase.

steps.title: LOWER and UPPER: which function to use
steps.lede: Choose the expression that converts a city name to all lower case for comparison.

steps.title: Trim, concat, and measure customer city names
steps.lede: Write a query that trims stray spaces from the city column, standardises its case, and builds a label column with CONCAT.

steps.title: Extracting date parts and computing elapsed days
steps.lede: Pull year, month, or hour from a date; subtract two dates to get the number of days between them.

blocks.text: EXTRACT(field FROM source) retrieves a subfield — year, month, day, hour — from a date or timestamp. EXTRACT(month FROM order_date) returns the month number an order was placed. Subtracting two dates gives the number of days between them: a later order_date minus an earlier one gives the elapsed days.

blocks.code:
SELECT order_id,
       order_date,
       EXTRACT(year  FROM order_date) AS order_year,
       EXTRACT(month FROM order_date) AS order_month,
       order_date - '2024-01-01'      AS days_since_jan1
  FROM orders
 LIMIT 5

annotations.text: EXTRACT(year FROM order_date) pulls the 4-digit year
EXTRACT(month FROM order_date) pulls the month number (1–12)
date - date gives the number of elapsed days as an integer

steps.lede: What does subtracting one date from another return in SQL?

steps.title: Type casting: CAST and :: syntax
steps.lede: Convert a value from one type to another using CAST or the :: shorthand.

blocks.text: PostgreSQL accepts two equivalent syntaxes for a type cast. CAST(expression AS type) is the standard form; expression::type is the shorthand. CAST(delivery_time_minutes AS text) and delivery_time_minutes::text both convert that numeric column to text — same result, two ways to write it.

A cast succeeds only if a suitable type conversion is defined between the source type and the target type. Converting delivery_time_minutes (an integer) to text works because an integer-to-text conversion is defined. A cast between two types with no defined conversion does not succeed.

left.code:
SELECT CAST(delivery_time_minutes AS text) AS minutes_text
  FROM orders
 LIMIT 3

annotations.text: Standard SQL CAST syntax: CAST(value AS target_type)

right.code:
SELECT delivery_time_minutes::text AS minutes_text
  FROM orders
 LIMIT 3

annotations.text: PostgreSQL shorthand: value::target_type — identical result

blocks.takeaway: Both expressions produce the same result. Use whichever your team's style guide prefers; the :: shorthand is common in PostgreSQL codebases.

steps.lede: Decide whether a given cast expression will succeed or fail based on whether a conversion is defined.

steps.title: Recap: Text, Dates, and Casts
steps.lede: Five string functions, two date operations, and two cast syntaxes.

blocks.text: LOWER and UPPER change string case; TRIM removes leading/trailing spaces; CONCAT joins strings (ignoring NULLs); LENGTH counts characters. EXTRACT(field FROM source) pulls a date subfield such as year or month; subtracting two dates gives elapsed days. CAST(expression AS type) and expression::type are two equivalent ways to convert a value to a different type — the cast succeeds only when a conversion between those types is defined.

blocks.title: Next: NULL Fallbacks and UNION
blocks.text: You can now transform values inside a query. Next you will handle missing values with COALESCE and combine the results of two queries into one list using UNION.

remediation_steps.title: LOWER and UPPER: converting string case
remediation_steps.lede: LOWER converts to all lower case; UPPER converts to all upper case.

blocks.text: LOWER(text) converts every character in the string to lower case: LOWER('LAGOS') → 'lagos', LOWER('Lagos') → 'lagos'. UPPER(text) converts every character to upper case: UPPER('lagos') → 'LAGOS'. These functions are useful when city names or other categorical values were entered with inconsistent casing and you need to compare or group them reliably.

remediation_steps.title: TRIM, CONCAT, and LENGTH
remediation_steps.lede: TRIM removes spaces; CONCAT joins strings; LENGTH counts characters.

blocks.text: TRIM removes the longest string of the given characters (a space by default) from the start, end, or both ends of a string. TRIM(city) strips accidental leading or trailing spaces from a city value. CONCAT joins its arguments into one string and ignores any NULL arguments: CONCAT(name, ' (', city, ')') builds a label even when city is NULL. LENGTH(text) returns the number of characters: LENGTH(name) gives the character count of a customer's name.

remediation_steps.title: Date subtraction gives elapsed days
remediation_steps.lede: Subtracting two dates returns the number of days between them.

blocks.text: Subtracting one date from another in SQL produces the number of days elapsed between them as an integer. If order_date is '2024-02-03' and you subtract '2024-01-01', the result is 33 days. This is different from EXTRACT, which pulls a single subfield (year, month, day) out of one date value.

remediation_steps.title: EXTRACT and date subtraction
remediation_steps.lede: EXTRACT pulls a subfield from one date; subtraction gives days between two dates.

blocks.text: EXTRACT(field FROM source) retrieves a single subfield from a date, time, timestamp, or interval value. The field can be year, month, day, hour, minute, second, and others. EXTRACT(month FROM order_date) returns the month number (1–12) for each order. To get the number of days between two dates, subtract them directly: order_date - '2024-01-01' gives elapsed days.

remediation_steps.title: When does a cast succeed?
remediation_steps.lede: A cast succeeds only when a conversion between the two types is defined.

blocks.text: A type cast succeeds only if a suitable conversion is defined between the source type and the target type. Converting an integer to text works because that conversion is defined. A cast between two types that have no defined conversion does not succeed — the database will return an error. Always check that the conversion you need is supported before relying on it in a query.

remediation_steps.title: Two cast syntaxes: CAST and ::
remediation_steps.lede: CAST(expression AS type) and expression::type are equivalent — use either.

blocks.text: PostgreSQL provides two equivalent syntaxes for a type cast. The standard form is CAST(expression AS type): CAST(delivery_time_minutes AS text). The shorthand is expression::type: delivery_time_minutes::text. Both produce exactly the same result. The :: shorthand is specific to PostgreSQL; CAST(... AS type) is portable across SQL dialects.

tiles.title: NULL Fallbacks and UNION
tiles.summary: Replace missing values with a default using COALESCE, and combine the results of two compatible queries into one list using UNION or UNION ALL.

steps.title: Replacing NULL with a default using COALESCE
steps.lede: COALESCE returns the first non-null argument — use it to substitute a default for missing values.

blocks.text: COALESCE(value [, ...]) returns the first of its arguments that is not null, and returns null only if every argument is null. COALESCE(city, 'unknown') returns the customer's actual city when it is recorded, and 'unknown' when it is missing. It is commonly used to substitute a default value for null — COALESCE(name, 'unnamed customer') falls back to a fixed label whenever a name was not recorded.

before.caption: Customers table — city is NULL for some rows

result_of.sql: SELECT customer_id, name, COALESCE(city, 'unknown') AS city FROM customers

blocks.change_summary: COALESCE(city, 'unknown') fills every NULL city with the fallback value 'unknown'.

steps.title: What does COALESCE return?
steps.lede: Predict the value returned by a COALESCE expression given a specific input.

steps.lede: Choose the COALESCE expression that replaces a missing customer name with a fixed label.

steps.title: Stacking query results with UNION and UNION ALL
steps.lede: UNION appends one result set to another; UNION removes duplicates while UNION ALL keeps every row.

blocks.text: UNION effectively appends the result rows of the second query to the result of the first, although there is no guarantee that this is the order the rows actually come back in. SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE city = 'Lagos' UNION SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 60 combines Lagos customers with customers who had a slow order into one list.

UNION eliminates duplicate rows from its combined result, the same way DISTINCT does, unless UNION ALL is used, which keeps every row. A Lagos customer who also placed two orders over 60 minutes appears once under UNION but three times under UNION ALL — once from the first query, twice from the second.

blocks.title: UNION vs UNION ALL
blocks.alt_text: Two query result sets stacked by UNION ALL (keeping the duplicate customer_id 1) and by UNION (removing the duplicate, leaving four distinct ids).

steps.title: UNION compatibility: matching columns and types
steps.lede: Both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible types.

blocks.text: For UNION, both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible data types. SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE city = 'Lagos' UNION SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 60 works because both return one integer column.

steps.title: Recap: NULL Fallbacks and UNION
steps.lede: COALESCE fills missing values; UNION stacks compatible result sets.

blocks.text: COALESCE(value [, ...]) returns the first non-null argument; use it to substitute a default for missing values. UNION appends the rows of the second query to the first — UNION removes duplicate rows, UNION ALL keeps every row. For UNION to work, both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible data types.

blocks.title: Next: Joining Tables
blocks.text: You can now combine rows from separate queries with UNION. Next you will combine columns from separate tables using JOIN — matching rows from an orders table to rows in a customers table on a shared key.

remediation_steps.title: How COALESCE picks its return value
remediation_steps.lede: COALESCE returns the first non-null argument, or null if all arguments are null.

blocks.text: COALESCE evaluates its arguments from left to right and returns the first one that is not null. COALESCE(city, 'unknown') returns city when city is not null, and 'unknown' when city is null. COALESCE returns null only when every argument is null — COALESCE(NULL, NULL) returns null.

remediation_steps.title: COALESCE as a default-value substitution
remediation_steps.lede: Use COALESCE(column, default) to replace NULL with a fixed fallback value.

blocks.text: COALESCE is commonly used to substitute a default value for null. COALESCE(name, 'unnamed customer') returns the customer's actual name when it is recorded, and the fixed string 'unnamed customer' when the name column is null. This pattern keeps downstream calculations and labels clean even when source data has gaps.

remediation_steps.title: UNION compatibility rules
remediation_steps.lede: Both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible types.

blocks.text: UNION requires both queries to return the same number of columns, with corresponding columns having compatible data types. If the first query returns one integer column and the second also returns one integer column, they are compatible. If the column counts differ, or if a text column is paired with an integer column, the UNION will fail.

remediation_steps.title: UNION vs UNION ALL: deduplication
remediation_steps.lede: UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps every row.

blocks.text: UNION appends the rows of the second query to the rows of the first. UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result, the same way DISTINCT does. UNION ALL keeps every row, including duplicates. Use UNION when you want a distinct list; use UNION ALL when you need every occurrence, including rows that appear in both queries.

steps.title: Combining two tables on a shared key
steps.lede: The customers table holds names; the orders table holds delivery times. To see both together, you join them.

blocks.text: QuickCart stores customer names in a customers table and delivery times in a separate orders table. Each orders row carries a customer_id that points back to customers. To see a customer's name alongside their delivery times, you need both tables combined into one result — that's what a JOIN does.

For each row of T1, an INNER JOIN produces a joined row for each row of T2 that satisfies the join condition; rows from either table with no match are dropped. The query SELECT c.name, o.delivery_time_minutes FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id pairs every customer row with every order row that shares its customer_id.

The join condition goes in an ON clause — a boolean expression like those used in WHERE — or in a USING clause when both tables share the same column name. ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id can be written USING (customer_id) when the column name is identical in both tables. INNER is the default: writing JOIN alone, without LEFT, RIGHT, or FULL, already means an INNER JOIN.

blocks.title: INNER JOIN: only matched rows survive

nodes.label: customer_id=3 (Fatima Aliyu) has no matching order — dropped from result
customer_id=4 has no matching order — dropped from result

blocks.alt_text: customers rows on the left, orders rows on the right. Rows with matching customer_id are linked. customer_id=3 (Fatima Aliyu) and customer_id=4 (Chidi Eze) have no matching order and are dropped from the result.

steps.title: INNER JOIN in action
Unmatched rows disappear
steps.lede: An inner join is strict: if one side has no match, that row is gone.

blocks.text: Because it's an inner join, a customer with zero orders — like customer_id 4 (Chidi Eze), who has no row in orders — produces no row at all in the result. Only customers who have at least one matching order appear.

steps.title: Which rows survive an INNER JOIN?
Write the JOIN condition
Joining on two columns at once
steps.lede: When a single column isn't enough to uniquely identify a match, you extend ON with AND.

blocks.text: The shipments table records, for each order_id and product_id pair, the date that item actually shipped. Matching shipments to order_items now needs two columns to agree at once — order_id alone isn't enough, because the same order can contain multiple products.

The ON clause takes a boolean expression of the same kind used in WHERE, so several column-equality tests can be combined with AND to require all of them to match before rows join. FROM order_items AS oi JOIN shipments AS s ON oi.order_id = s.order_id AND oi.product_id = s.product_id joins a shipment row only to the order_items row for the exact same order and the exact same product.

USING is a shorthand when both tables share the same column names: USING (a, b) expands to ON T1.a = T2.a AND T1.b = T2.b. Since order_items and shipments both use order_id and product_id, that same join can be written FROM order_items JOIN shipments USING (order_id, product_id).

blocks.code:
-- ON form: two equality tests combined with AND
SELECT oi.order_id, oi.product_id, s.shipped_date
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN shipments AS s
  ON oi.order_id = s.order_id
 AND oi.product_id = s.product_id;

-- USING form: shorthand when column names match on both sides
SELECT order_id, product_id, s.shipped_date
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN shipments AS s
  USING (order_id, product_id);

annotations.text: ON with AND: both order_id AND product_id must match
USING: shorthand — expands to the same two-column condition

Keeping unmatched rows with LEFT JOIN
steps.lede: An inner join drops customers with no orders. A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer, filling missing order columns with NULL.

blocks.text: An inner join between customers and orders drops any customer with zero orders. To list every customer — including those who haven't ordered yet — you need an outer join.

A LEFT OUTER JOIN performs an inner join, then adds a row for each row of T1 with no match in T2, filling T2's columns with NULL. SELECT c.name, o.delivery_time_minutes FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id lists every customer; delivery_time_minutes is NULL for any customer with no orders.

blocks.title: LEFT JOIN vs INNER JOIN
blocks.alt_text: LEFT JOIN: customer_id=1 matches order 1001 normally. Customers 4 and 5 have no orders — they appear in the result with NULL in the delivery_time_minutes column. An INNER JOIN would have dropped them entirely.

steps.title: RIGHT, FULL, and the optional OUTER keyword
steps.lede: LEFT JOIN keeps every left-side row. RIGHT and FULL extend that logic to the other side or both sides.

blocks.text: A RIGHT OUTER JOIN is the converse of a left join: it keeps every row of T2, NULL-filling T1's columns for rows of T2 with no match. A FULL OUTER JOIN performs an inner join, then adds NULL-filled rows for the unmatched rows of both T1 and T2 — so no row from either table is lost.
INNER and OUTER are both optional keywords. LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL each already imply an outer join even without writing OUTER, so LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN mean exactly the same thing.

steps.lede: Three join patterns cover most real-world needs.

blocks.text: INNER JOIN keeps only rows with a match on both sides. Extend ON with AND to match on multiple columns, or use USING when the column names are identical. LEFT JOIN keeps every left-side row and NULL-fills the right side for unmatched rows; RIGHT and FULL extend that logic. OUTER is always optional.

blocks.title: Up next: Query Execution Order
blocks.text: SQL clauses are written in one order but processed in another — FROM first, SELECT last. Next you'll trace that order and learn where aliases can and cannot be used.

remediation_steps.title: Which rows survive: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Compare what an INNER JOIN keeps versus what it drops.

blocks.text: customers has six rows (customer_id 1–6). orders has rows for customer_id 1, 2, and 3 only. An INNER JOIN ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id produces rows only for customers 1, 2, and 3 — the ones with at least one matching order. Customers 4, 5, and 6 have no matching order row, so they are dropped entirely from the result. The rule: a row survives only if both sides have a match.

remediation_steps.title: Extending ON with AND: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: See what changes when you add a second condition to ON.

blocks.text: Single-column join: FROM order_items AS oi JOIN shipments AS s ON oi.order_id = s.order_id — this matches every shipment for the same order, even if the product_id differs. Composite join: ON oi.order_id = s.order_id AND oi.product_id = s.product_id — now both columns must agree. Only the shipment for the exact same order and the exact same product is joined. The ON clause accepts any boolean expression, so AND works the same way it does in WHERE.

remediation_steps.title: LEFT JOIN vs INNER JOIN: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: The same query with JOIN versus LEFT JOIN gives very different row counts.

blocks.text: INNER JOIN: SELECT c.name, o.delivery_time_minutes FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id — returns only customers 1, 2, and 3, who have orders. Customers 4 and 5 are dropped. LEFT JOIN: replace JOIN with LEFT JOIN — now all six customers appear. Customers 4 and 5 get a row with delivery_time_minutes = NULL. The left table (customers) always contributes at least one row to the result.

tiles.title: Query Execution Order and Subqueries in WHERE

steps.title: SQL clauses run in a different order than you write them
steps.lede: You write SELECT first, but the database processes FROM first. Knowing the real order explains many surprising errors.

blocks.text: A query like SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 0 GROUP BY customer_id HAVING AVG(delivery_time_minutes) > 30 ORDER BY avg_time DESC is written top to bottom, SELECT first — but that is not the order it is logically processed in.

In a SELECT's general processing order, the FROM list is computed first, then WHERE eliminates non-matching rows, then GROUP BY groups the rows and HAVING eliminates groups, then the SELECT output expressions are computed, and ORDER BY sorts the rows last. In the query above: orders is read, rows with delivery_time_minutes ≤ 0 are dropped, the remaining rows are grouped by customer_id, groups with an average ≤ 30 are removed, the SELECT computes avg_time, and ORDER BY sorts by it.

blocks.title: SQL clause processing order
blocks.alt_text: Six steps left to right: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. Each step feeds the next.

steps.title: Tracing the processing order
Where an alias can — and cannot — be used
steps.lede: SELECT runs after WHERE and HAVING, so an alias defined in SELECT isn't visible to those clauses.

blocks.text: An output column's alias, assigned with AS in the SELECT list, can be referred to in ORDER BY and GROUP BY, but not in WHERE or HAVING — those clauses run before SELECT, so the alias doesn't exist yet. In the example query, WHERE avg_time > 30 would fail; the expression must be written out in HAVING as AVG(delivery_time_minutes) > 30.

steps.title: Trace the clause processing order
Fix the alias placement
Using a query result as a filter value
steps.lede: When the filter value itself must be computed — like the average delivery time — you embed a query inside WHERE.

blocks.text: Suppose you want the orders that took longer than the average delivery time across all orders. You don't know that average ahead of time — it has to be computed by another query, used right inside the WHERE clause.

A subquery that returns a single (scalar) value can be used as a value expression in a comparison. SELECT order_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > (SELECT AVG(delivery_time_minutes) FROM orders) keeps only the orders slower than the overall average — the inner SELECT computes that one number, and the outer WHERE compares each row's delivery time against it.

A subquery can also appear as the right side of IN: WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40) keeps rows whose customer_id value is found in the subquery's result. SELECT name FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40) finds the customers who have placed at least one order slower than 40 minutes.

blocks.code:
-- Scalar subquery: inner query returns one value
SELECT order_id, delivery_time_minutes
FROM orders
WHERE delivery_time_minutes > (
    SELECT AVG(delivery_time_minutes)
    FROM orders
);

-- IN subquery: inner query returns a list of values
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (
    SELECT customer_id
    FROM orders
    WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40
);

annotations.text: Inner query: computes one average value
Inner query: returns a list of customer_ids with slow orders

steps.title: Subqueries inside WHERE
Write a scalar subquery comparison
Filter with IN and a scalar subquery
Execution order and WHERE subqueries
steps.lede: Two ideas that explain how SQL really runs.

blocks.text: SQL processes clauses in this order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. An alias defined in SELECT is visible in ORDER BY and GROUP BY, but not in WHERE or HAVING. A subquery in WHERE can return a single value for a comparison or a list of values for IN — the inner query runs first and its result is used by the outer WHERE.

blocks.title: Up next: Subqueries in FROM and CTEs
blocks.text: A subquery can also appear in FROM, acting as a virtual table. CTEs let you name that virtual table once with WITH and reuse it — making complex queries easier to read.

remediation_steps.title: The processing order: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Compare the written order of clauses with the order they actually run.

blocks.text: Written order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY. Processing order: FROM (read orders), WHERE (drop rows with delivery_time_minutes ≤ 0), GROUP BY (group by customer_id), HAVING (drop groups with average ≤ 30), SELECT (compute avg_time alias), ORDER BY (sort by avg_time). SELECT runs fifth — not first. That's why an alias defined in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE or HAVING.

remediation_steps.title: Scalar subquery in WHERE: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Compare a hard-coded filter value with one computed by a subquery.

blocks.text: Hard-coded: WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 35 — works, but 35 is a guess. Scalar subquery: WHERE delivery_time_minutes > (SELECT AVG(delivery_time_minutes) FROM orders) — the inner query computes the actual average from the data and returns one number; the outer WHERE compares each row against that number. The subquery must return exactly one value to be used in a comparison like > or =.

tiles.title: Subqueries in FROM and Common Table Expressions

steps.title: Treating a query result as a table
steps.lede: Sometimes the thing you want to filter isn't a real table — it's the result of an aggregate query. A subquery in FROM lets you query that result.

blocks.text: Sometimes the thing you want to filter or select from isn't a real table at all, but the result of an aggregate query — like each customer's own average delivery time, treated as if it were a table you could query further.

A subquery used in FROM must be enclosed in parentheses and is typically given a table alias: FROM (SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) AS customer_avg. The SQL standard requires this alias; while PostgreSQL allows it to be omitted, writing one is good practice for portability.

blocks.code:
SELECT customer_id, avg_time
FROM (
    SELECT customer_id,
           AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
) AS customer_avg
WHERE avg_time > 30;

annotations.text: Inner query: computes per-customer average; aliased as customer_avg
Outer query: reads avg_time from the virtual table customer_avg
Outer WHERE: filters using avg_time — the alias the inner query defined

steps.title: Inner column names become the virtual table's columns
steps.lede: The outer query sees the inner query's output columns by their names or aliases.

blocks.text: When a SELECT is used as a subquery, the name of each of its output columns — its own column name or its AS alias — is seen by the outer query as the column name of the virtual table the subquery produces. That's why the outer query can refer to avg_time directly: it's the alias the inner query already gave that column.

steps.title: Subqueries in FROM
Use inner output columns in the outer query
Write a FROM subquery with an alias
Naming a query once with WITH
steps.lede: A CTE lets you define a named result set at the top of a query and read it by name — like a temporary table that exists just for that query.

blocks.text: The customer_avg subquery from before works, but naming it once up front — instead of burying it inside FROM — can make a longer query easier to read.

WITH provides a way to write one or more auxiliary statements — Common Table Expressions (CTEs) — that can be thought of as defining temporary tables that exist just for one query. A CTE is written as WITH name AS (query), and the primary statement then reads it by name, as if it were a table: WITH customer_avg AS (SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT customer_id, avg_time FROM customer_avg WHERE avg_time > 30.

A second CTE can read from the first: define customer_avg, then define slow_customers AS (SELECT customer_id FROM customer_avg WHERE avg_time > 30), then have the primary query read from slow_customers. Breaking a complex query into named CTEs with WITH is an alternative to nested subqueries, and can make the query easier to follow.

blocks.code:
WITH customer_avg AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
slow_customers AS (
    SELECT customer_id
    FROM customer_avg
    WHERE avg_time > 30
)
SELECT c.name, ca.avg_time
FROM customers AS c
JOIN slow_customers AS sc ON c.customer_id = sc.customer_id
JOIN customer_avg AS ca ON c.customer_id = ca.customer_id;

annotations.text: First CTE: customer_avg — per-customer average delivery time
Second CTE: slow_customers — reads from customer_avg
Primary query: reads from both CTEs by name

steps.title: WITH: naming a query once, then reading it like a table
Rewrite a nested subquery as a CTE
Write a WITH clause
Subqueries in FROM and CTEs
steps.lede: Two ways to treat a query result as a named table.

blocks.text: A subquery in FROM must be wrapped in parentheses and should be given an alias (the SQL standard requires it, though PostgreSQL allows omission); the outer query reads its output columns by name. A CTE (WITH name AS (query)) names that same idea at the top of the query, making it reusable and easier to read. A second CTE can read from the first; the primary query reads from any CTE by name.

remediation_steps.title: Inner column names: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: See what happens when the outer query uses a column name the inner query didn't define.

blocks.text: Inner query defines: SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id. The virtual table has two columns: customer_id and avg_time. Outer query — correct: SELECT customer_id, avg_time FROM (...) AS customer_avg WHERE avg_time > 30. Outer query — wrong: WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 30 — delivery_time_minutes is not a column of the virtual table; the inner query aggregated it away. The outer query can only see the columns the inner query outputs.

remediation_steps.title: Nested subquery vs CTE: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: The same logic written as a nested subquery and as a CTE.

blocks.text: Nested subquery: SELECT customer_id, avg_time FROM (SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) AS customer_avg WHERE avg_time > 30. CTE equivalent: WITH customer_avg AS (SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT customer_id, avg_time FROM customer_avg WHERE avg_time > 30. Both produce the same result. The CTE names the inner query once at the top; the nested form buries it inside FROM. CTEs are an alternative to nested subqueries and can make the query easier to follow.
